def peak_potential_irreversible(
    v: float | ArrayLike,
    k0: float,
    E0_prime: float = 0.0,
    D: float = 1e-5,
    alpha: float = 0.5,
    n_alpha: float = 1,
    T: float = STANDARD_TEMPERATURE,
    R: float = GAS_CONSTANT,
    F: float = FARADAY,
    scan_direction: Literal["cathodic", "anodic"] = "cathodic",
) -> float | np.ndarray:
    r"""Compute peak potential for totally irreversible electron transfer.

    Calculates the peak potential :math:`E_p` as a function of scan rate :math:`v`
    under totally irreversible charge-transfer kinetics (Bard & Faulkner Eq. 6.3.18):

    .. math::

        E_p = E^{0\prime} \mp \frac{R T}{\alpha n_\alpha F} \left[ 0.780 + \frac{1}{2} \ln\left( \frac{\alpha n_\alpha F D v}{R T (k^0)^2} \right) \right]

    (negative sign for cathodic reduction, positive sign for anodic oxidation with
    :math:`(1-\alpha)`).

    The diagnostic shift per decade of scan rate is:

    .. math::

        \frac{\partial E_p}{\partial \log_{10} v} = \mp \frac{2.3026 R T}{2 \alpha n_\alpha F} \approx \mp \frac{29.6}{\alpha n_\alpha}\,\text{mV/decade at } 25^\circ\text{C}

    Parameters
    ----------
    v : float or array-like
        Potential sweep scan rate in :math:`\text{V}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}` (:math:`v > 0`).
    k0 : float
        Heterogeneous standard rate constant :math:`k^0 > 0`.
    E0_prime : float, default 0.0
        Formal electrode potential :math:`E^{0\prime}` in Volts.
    D : float, default 1e-5
        Diffusion coefficient (:math:`D > 0`).
    alpha : float, default 0.5
        Charge transfer coefficient (:math:`0 < \alpha < 1`).
    n_alpha : float, default 1
        Number of electrons in rate-determining step (:math:`n_\alpha > 0`).
    T : float, default 298.15
        Thermodynamic temperature in Kelvin (:math:`T > 0`).
    R : float, default 8.31446
        Molar gas constant (:math:`R > 0`).
    F : float, default 96485.332
        Faraday constant (:math:`F > 0`).
    scan_direction : {"cathodic", "anodic"}, default "cathodic"
        Direction of sweep ("cathodic" or "anodic").

    Returns
    -------
    float or numpy.ndarray
        Peak potential :math:`E_p` in Volts.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If parameters are non-positive or outside physical limits.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> from softpotato.analytical.voltammetry import peak_potential_irreversible
    >>> ep = peak_potential_irreversible(0.1, k0=1e-4, E0_prime=0.0)
    >>> round(ep, 4)
    -0.2347
    """
    _validate_positive(k0, "Standard rate constant k0")
    _validate_positive(D, "Diffusion coefficient D")
    _validate_alpha(alpha)
    _validate_positive(n_alpha, "Number of electrons n_alpha")
    _validate_positive(T, "Temperature T")
    _validate_positive(R, "Gas constant R")
    _validate_positive(F, "Faraday constant F")

    if scan_direction not in ("cathodic", "anodic"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Invalid scan_direction: {scan_direction!r}. Must be 'cathodic' or 'anodic'."
        )

    v_arr = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)
    if np.any(v_arr <= 0):
        raise ValueError(f"Scan rate v must be strictly positive (v > 0), got {v!r}.")

    eff_alpha = alpha if scan_direction == "cathodic" else (1.0 - alpha)
    shift_arg = (eff_alpha * n_alpha * F * D * v_arr) / (R * T * (k0**2))
    bracket = 0.780 + 0.5 * np.log(shift_arg)
    slope_term = (R * T) / (eff_alpha * n_alpha * F)

    if scan_direction == "cathodic":
        ep = E0_prime - slope_term * bracket
    else:
        ep = E0_prime + slope_term * bracket

    return _format_output(ep, np.ndim(v) == 0)

docs.title: Decoding Simulation Jargon: A Modeler’s Guide for Experimental Electrochemists
docs.text:
If you have ever talked to a computational chemist or read a modeling paper, you have likely run into terms like mesh generation, Dirichlet boundaries, stiff solvers, and post-processing.

While modelers make these concepts sound like an entirely separate branch of science, the simulation workflow directly mirrors what you already do in the wet lab. Setting up differential equations is simply preparing a virtual electrochemical cell, running a virtual potentiostat, and analyzing the resulting data.

docs.title: Pre-Processing (Setting Up the Experiment)
docs.text: In computational science, pre-processing encompasses everything you do before pressing "run." In the lab, this is equivalent to polishing your glassy carbon electrode, preparing your supporting electrolyte, bubbling argon to deoxygenate the cell, and programming your potentiostat parameters.

docs.title: Domain Definition & Geometry
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Physical domain, geometry, coordinate system (1D planar, 2D axisymmetric, 3D).
  • What it means at the bench: Choosing your cell architecture and electrode shape.
  • In practice: If you are running cyclic voltammetry on a standard macrodisk electrode over short times, diffusion is planar and perpendicular to the surface. Modelers simplify this to a one-dimensional line (1D) extending from the electrode surface into the bulk electrolyte. For a microdisk where radial diffusion dominates, they use a two-dimensional axisymmetric coordinate system.

docs.title: Parameterization
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Parameter specification, physical constants, transport coefficients.
  • What it means at the bench: Your chemical recipe and experimental constants.
  • In practice: This is where you input bulk analyte concentration (\(C^*\)), diffusion coefficients (\(D\)), temperature (\(T\)), standard heterogeneous rate constants (\(k^0\)), transfer coefficients (\(\alpha\)), and scan rate (\(\nu\)).

docs.title: Grid Generation & Meshing
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Spatial discretization, meshing, non-uniform/expanding grid.
  • What it means at the bench: Deciding where to observe the solution in fine detail.
  • In practice: A computer cannot track an infinite number of points in space, so it slices the distance between the electrode and the bulk into discrete boxes or nodes. Because concentration gradients change violently within the first few micrometers of the electrode surface, modelers place dense, tightly spaced points near the interface (fine grid) and gradually expand the spacing further out into the bulk where concentration remains uniform.

docs.title: Initial Conditions (ICs)
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: \(t = 0\) state, initial value assignment.
  • What it means at the bench: The state of your beaker right before you hit "start" on your potentiostat.
  • In practice: At \(t = 0\), before any potential is applied, the concentration of your redox species is uniform everywhere (\(C(x, 0) = C^*\)), the product concentration is typically zero, and no concentration gradients exist.

docs.title: Boundary Conditions (BCs)
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundary conditions.
  • What it means at the bench: What physically happens at the boundaries of your cell (the electrode interface and the far-away bulk).
  • In practice:
  • The Bulk Solution (Far Boundary): Far away from the electrode, the solution remains untouched. Modelers set this as a fixed concentration boundary (Dirichlet condition) or assume no concentration gradient changes there.
  • Cell Walls / Insulating Shrouds: Electroactive species cannot pass through glass walls or the Kel-F/Teflon shroud of a disk electrode. Modelers enforce a zero-flux condition (Neumann condition), meaning flux across the boundary equals zero.
  • The Working Electrode Surface: This is where chemistry occurs. Under reversible (Nernstian) conditions, the surface ratio of oxidized and reduced species is fixed by the potential (Dirichlet). Under quasi-reversible kinetics, the flux of molecules reacting at the surface depends directly on the Butler-Volmer equation linking current, potential, and concentration (Robin / mixed condition).

docs.title: Solving (Running the Experiment)
docs.text: Once pre-processing is complete, the software runs the simulation. This is the computational equivalent of your potentiostat executing a potential scan while logging current.

docs.title: Time Discretization & Time-Stepping
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Time integrator, \(\Delta t\), Runge-Kutta, Crank-Nicolson, backward differentiation formulas (BDF).
  • What it means at the bench: The sampling rate of your potentiostat.
  • In practice: Just as a potentiostat records current at specific sampling intervals (e.g., every 1 mV or every 10 ms), the computer advances time in discrete steps (\(\Delta t\)), calculating how diffusion and reactions evolve from one slice of time to the next.

docs.title: Matrix Assembly & Equation Solving
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Linear/non-linear algebraic solver, Newton-Raphson iterations, matrix inversion.
  • What it means at the bench: The internal hardware processing current-voltage signals.
  • In practice: The governing differential equations (like Fick's second law coupled with Butler-Volmer kinetics) are converted into large systems of algebraic equations. The solver balances the equations at every grid point simultaneously to determine the exact concentration of each chemical species.

docs.title: Convergence & Residual Tracking
docs.text:
• What modelers call it: Convergence criteria, tolerances, residual norms.
  • What it means at the bench: Checking whether your potentiostat overloaded or your scan was noisy.
  • In practice: At each time step, the solver checks whether the calculated concentrations satisfy mass conservation and kinetic laws within a tiny error tolerance (e.g., \(10^{-6}\)). If the solution stabilizes and errors shrink, the step "converged." If it diverges, the time step was likely too large or the spatial grid was too coarse.

docs.title: Post-Processing (Analyzing the Data)
docs.text: Post-processing is everything that happens after the calculation finishes: transforming raw numerical values into standard electrochemical figures.

docs.title: Flux Extraction & Current Calculation
docs.text:
• What it means: The solver tracks concentration profiles across space, not electrical currents directly.
  • The translation: Using Faraday's Law, the post-processor takes the concentration gradient of the electroactive species right at the electrode boundary (\(x = 0\)), calculates the molar flux (\(J = -D \frac{\partial C}{\partial x}\)), and converts that flux into measurable current:

$$ I = n F A J $$

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: • What it means: Plotting cyclic voltammograms (\(I\) vs. \(E\)), chronoamperometry transients (\(I\) vs. \(t\)), or spatial concentration snapshots showing the diffusion layer growing out from the electrode into the solution.

docs.title: Derived Metrics
docs.text: • What it means: Extracting peak potentials (\(E_p\)), peak currents (\(i_p\)), half-wave potentials (\(E_{1/2}\)), or integrating current over time to obtain charge (\(Q\)).

docs.title: Verification and Validation (Quality Control)
docs.text:
Before trusting any simulation output, computational modelers perform two distinct sanity checks:

  • Verification ("Solving the equations right"): Checking that the math and code are bug-free. In electrochemistry, this is typically done by running a test case with fast kinetics and comparing the output against classical analytical solutions, such as the Cottrell equation for potential steps or the Randles-Sevcik equation for reversible cyclic voltammetry. If the numerical model reproduces the theoretical peak current within a specified tolerance, say 0.1%, the code is verified.
  • Validation ("Solving the right equations"): Comparing the simulated curves against actual bench data collected from your real electrochemical cell (e.g., testing standard ferrocene or ferricyanide solutions). If the simulated peak-to-peak splitting and current heights match your experimental data across multiple scan rates, the physical model is validated.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text: Stage Computational Term Wet-Lab Equivalent Pre-Processing Domain, Grid, Parameters, ICs, BCs Cell geometry, mesh resolution, analyte concentrations, starting potential, electrode boundaries Solving Time-stepping, Newton solvers, Convergence Potentiostat sampling, potential sweep execution, signal stability Post-Processing Gradient extraction, Faraday conversion, Plotting Converting diffusion flux to current (\(I = nFAJ\)), plotting CVs, extracting peak potentials Verification Benchmark against analytical equations Checking if reversible simulations match Cottrell or Randles-Sevcik theory Validation Benchmarking against experimental data Overlaying simulated voltammograms onto real experimental scans

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Electrochemical theory and numerical modelling fundamentals behind Soft Potato.

These conceptual guides bridge laboratory intuition (potentials, currents, diffusion layers, and reaction mechanisms) with numerical simulation (meshes, finite-difference operators, time integrators, and analytical benchmarks)—without burying you in boilerplate code.

docs.title: Electrochemistry
docs.text:
• Electrode Kinetics

    Nernst equilibrium vs. Butler–Volmer and Tafel kinetics (\(E^{0\prime}\), \(k^0\), \(\alpha\)), reversibility regimes (\(\Lambda\), \(\Psi\)), and IUPAC sign conventions.

  • Mass Transport

    Planar, spherical, cylindrical, and microelectrode diffusion, plus forced convection–diffusion at a Rotating Disk Electrode (RDE).

  • Reaction Mechanisms

    Coupled heterogeneous electron transfer and homogeneous solution chemistry: E, EC, EE, and catalytic EC' mechanisms.

docs.title: Numerical Modelling
docs.text:
• Spatial Grids & Meshes

    Discretizing the diffusion layer \(\delta = 6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}\) with Uniform1DMesh, ExponentialMesh, and GeometricExpandingMesh.

  • Time-Stepping & Solvers

    Explicit (FTCS), Implicit (BTCS), Crank–Nicolson, and Method-of-Lines (ScipyIVPSolver), CFL stability, and piecewise event_times integration.

  • Benchmarking & Validation

    Verifying spatial/temporal convergence orders and validating solvers against closed-form analytical solutions via softpotato.analytical.benchmark.

  • API Reference: Full class and function signatures across all Soft Potato modules.

docs.title: Electrode Kinetics
docs.text:
Interfacial electron transfer governs how rapidly an oxidized species \(\text{Ox}\) and a reduced species \(\text{Red}\) exchange electrons at an electrode surface:

\[ \text{Ox} + n e^- \underset{k_b(E)}{\overset{k_f(E)}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{Red} \]

In Soft Potato, you choose between thermodynamic equilibrium (NernstianEquilibrium) and finite-rate kinetics (ButlerVolmer, TafelKinetics), depending on whether electron transfer is fast or rate-limiting relative to mass transport.

docs.title: Sign Convention (IUPAC)
docs.text:
Soft Potato follows the IUPAC convention by default (anodic_positive=True):

  • Anodic (oxidation) current is positive (\(I > 0\) when \(E > E^{0\prime}\), net \(\text{Red} \to \text{Ox}\)).
  • Cathodic (reduction) current is negative (\(I < 0\) when \(E < E^{0\prime}\), net \(\text{Ox} \to \text{Red}\)).

For an interfacial reduction flux \(J = k_f(E)\,c_{\text{Ox}}(0, t) - k_b(E)\,c_{\text{Red}}(0, t)\), the Faradaic current density is:

\[ j = -n F J = n F \left[ k_b(E)\,c_{\text{Red}}(0, t) - k_f(E)\,c_{\text{Ox}}(0, t) \right] \]

docs.title: Nernst Equilibrium (NernstianEquilibrium)
docs.text:
When the heterogeneous rate constant \(k^0\) is much faster than the rate of mass transport, the electrode interface remains in local thermodynamic equilibrium at all times. The surface concentrations are locked to the applied potential \(E(t)\) by the Nernst equation:

\[ E(t) = E^{0\prime} + \frac{R T}{n F} \ln \frac{c_{\text{Ox}}(0, t)}{c_{\text{Red}}(0, t)} \]

Equivalently, defining the dimensionless potential \(\theta = \frac{n F}{R T}(E - E^{0\prime})\), the surface ratio is:

\[ \frac{c_{\text{Ox}}(0, t)}{c_{\text{Red}}(0, t)} = \exp(\theta) \]

In a simulation, NernstianEquilibrium enforces this ratio as a Dirichlet-like coupled boundary condition at the electrode surface (\(x = 0\)), assuming equal diffusivities or flux balance \(D_{\text{Ox}} \partial_x c_{\text{Ox}} + D_{\text{Red}} \partial_x c_{\text{Red}} = 0\).

docs.title: Butler–Volmer Kinetics (ButlerVolmer)
docs.text:
When electron transfer has a finite barrier, surface concentrations deviate from Nernstian equilibrium and the net flux is governed by the Butler–Volmer rate constants:

\[ k_f(E) = k^0 \exp\!\left[-\frac{\alpha n F}{R T}(E - E^{0\prime})\right], \qquad k_b(E) = k^0 \exp\!\left[\frac{(1 - \alpha) n F}{R T}(E - E^{0\prime})\right] \]

where:

  • \(E^{0\prime}\) (\(\text{V}\)) is the formal reduction potential.
  • \(k^0\) (\(\text{m}/\text{s}\)) is the standard heterogeneous rate constant (evaluated at \(E = E^{0\prime}\)).
  • \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\) is the cathodic charge-transfer coefficient (often \(\approx 0.5\) for symmetric barriers).
  • \(\eta = E - E^{0\prime}\) is the overpotential (relative to \(E^{0\prime}\), or relative to \(E_{\text{eq}}\) when \(c_{\text{Ox}}^* \neq c_{\text{Red}}^*\)).

At equilibrium (\(E = E_{\text{eq}}\), \(j = 0\)), both opposing branches equal the exchange current density \(j_0\):

\[ j_0 = n F k^0 \left(c_{\text{Ox}}^*\right)^{1-\alpha} \left(c_{\text{Red}}^*\right)^{\alpha} \]

In a simulation, ButlerVolmer translates \(k_f(E)\) and \(k_b(E)\) into Robin / Neumann flux boundary conditions at \(x = 0\):

\[ D_{\text{Ox}} \left.\frac{\partial c_{\text{Ox}}}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} = k_f(E)\,c_{\text{Ox}}(0, t) - k_b(E)\,c_{\text{Red}}(0, t) \]

docs.title: Tafel Limit (TafelKinetics)
docs.text:
At large overpotentials (\(|\eta| \gg \frac{R T}{n F} \approx 25.7\text{ mV}\) at \(298\text{ K}\)), the reverse reaction becomes negligible. The Butler–Volmer equation simplifies to the exponential Tafel relation:

\[ \eta = a + b \log_{10} |j|, \qquad |b_{\text{cathodic}}| = \frac{2.303\,R T}{\alpha n F}, \qquad |b_{\text{anodic}}| = \frac{2.303\,R T}{(1 - \alpha) n F} \]

At \(298\text{ K}\) with \(n = 1\) and \(\alpha = 0.5\), the classic Tafel slope is \(\approx 118\text{ mV}/\text{decade}\).

docs.title: Reversibility Regimes
docs.text:
Electrochemical "reversibility" is not an intrinsic property of a molecule alone—it is a competition between electron-transfer kinetics (\(k^0\)) and the experimental timescale (such as scan rate \(v\) in cyclic voltammetry, or rotation rate \(\omega\) in RDE).

For cyclic voltammetry, Matsuda and Ayabe defined the dimensionless parameter \(\Lambda\), and Nicholson defined \(\Psi\):

\[ \Lambda = \frac{k^0}{\sqrt{\frac{n F v D}{R T}}}, \qquad \Psi = \gamma^\alpha \frac{k^0}{\sqrt{\pi \frac{n F v D}{R T}}}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{D_{\text{Ox}}}{D_{\text{Red}}} \] Regime Matsuda–Ayabe \(\Lambda\) CV Peak Separation \(\Delta E_p\) (\(298\text{ K}\)) Peak Current Scaling Best Model in Soft Potato Reversible \(\Lambda \gtrsim 15\) \(\Delta E_p \approx \frac{59\text{ mV}}{n}\) (independent of \(v\)) \(I_p \propto v^{1/2}\) (Randles–Ševčík) NernstianEquilibrium or ButlerVolmer with large \(k^0\) Quasi-reversible \(10^{-2(1+\alpha)} \lesssim \Lambda \lesssim 15\) \(\Delta E_p > \frac{59\text{ mV}}{n}\) (grows with \(v\)) Non-linear in \(v^{1/2}\); shifted peaks ButlerVolmer (\(k^0, \alpha, E^{0\prime}\)) Irreversible \(\Lambda \lesssim 10^{-2(1+\alpha)}\) Reverse peak absent; \(E_p\) shifts by \(\frac{29.6\text{ mV}}{\alpha n}\) per decade of \(v\) \(I_p \propto v^{1/2}\) (with \(\sqrt{\alpha}\) factor) ButlerVolmer (small \(k^0\)) or TafelKinetics

Laboratory Intuition: Slowing Down vs. Speeding Up

Increasing the scan rate \(v\) shrinks the diffusion layer (\(\delta \propto v^{-1/2}\)) and increases the diffusive flux. A redox couple that looks reversible at \(10\text{ mV/s}\) can become quasi-reversible at \(10\text{ V/s}\) because mass transport outpaces \(k^0\).

docs.title: Reaction Mechanisms
docs.text:
Real electrochemical systems often involve more than a single electron transfer: electrogenerated intermediates can react in solution, undergo a second electron transfer, or regenerate the starting material. Soft Potato models these coupled systems using Mechanism, combining heterogeneous ElectrochemicalStep boundaries with homogeneous ReactionNetwork terms in the reaction–diffusion PDE:

\[ \frac{\partial c_i}{\partial t} = D_i \nabla^2 c_i + R_i(\mathbf{c}, x, t) \]

where \(R_i(\mathbf{c}, x, t)\) is the net volumetric production/consumption rate of species \(i\) from all homogeneous reactions.

docs.title: Canonical Mechanisms
docs.text:
In electrochemical nomenclature, E denotes a heterogeneous electron transfer at the electrode surface, and C denotes a homogeneous chemical reaction in solution.

Mechanism Reaction Scheme Typical Voltammetric Signature Soft Potato Building Blocks E \(\text{Ox} + n e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}\) Classic reversible or quasi-reversible CV peaks (\(I_{pa}/I_{pc} = 1\) for equal \(D\)). ElectrochemicalStep(ox, red, kinetics) EC \(\text{Ox} + n e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}\)\(\text{Red} \xrightarrow{k_c} \text{P}\) Reverse (anodic) peak shrinks or disappears as \(k_c / v\) increases; forward peak shifts positively. ElectrochemicalStep + FirstOrderReaction(red, P, k=...) (or ReversibleReaction) EE \(\text{A} + n_1 e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{B}\) (\(E_1^0\))\(\text{B} + n_2 e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{C}\) (\(E_2^0\)) Two distinct waves if \(E_1^0 - E_2^0 \gg \frac{RT}{F}\), merging into a single multi-electron wave when \(E_2^0 \ge E_1^0\). Two ElectrochemicalSteps in Mechanism (or disproportionation \(2\text{B} \rightleftharpoons \text{A} + \text{C}\) via DisproportionationReaction) EC' (Catalytic) \(\text{Ox} + n e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}\)\(\text{Red} + \text{Z} \xrightarrow{k_{\text{cat}}} \text{Ox} + \text{P}\) Forward current is amplified into a sigmoidal plateau (\(I_{\text{cat}} \propto \sqrt{k_{\text{cat}}}\)) while the reverse peak vanishes. ElectrochemicalStep + CatalyticReaction

docs.title: How Mechanisms Map to the PDE
1. Heterogeneous Steps (E)
docs.text:
Each ElectrochemicalStep applies only at the electrode boundary (\(x = 0\), or electrode_side="right"). It does not appear in \(R_i(\mathbf{c}, x, t)\) inside the bulk solution; instead, it sets the surface flux or concentration ratio for the coupled ox/red pair.

  • For an EE mechanism (\(\text{A} \rightleftharpoons \text{B} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}\)), the intermediate \(\text{B}\) participates in two boundary conditions simultaneously: its net interfacial flux is the sum of the reduction flux from \(\text{A} \to \text{B}\) and the oxidation/reduction flux from \(\text{B} \to \text{C}\).

docs.title: 2. Homogeneous Steps (C)
docs.text:
Each HomogeneousReaction (such as FirstOrderReaction, SecondOrderReaction, ReversibleReaction, CatalyticReaction, DimerizationReaction, DisproportionationReaction, or CustomReaction) contributes to the volumetric source term \(R_i(\mathbf{c}, x, t)\) at every interior grid node.

For example, in an EC mechanism where \( ext{Red} \xrightarrow{k_c} ext{P}\):

\[ rac{\partial c_{ ext{Ox}}}{\partial t} = D_{ ext{Ox}} abla^2 c_{ ext{Ox}}, \qquad rac{\partial c_{ ext{Red}}}{\partial t} = D_{ ext{Red}} abla^2 c_{ ext{Red}} - k_c \, c_{ ext{Red}}, \qquad rac{\partial c_{ ext{P}}}{\partial t} = D_{ ext{P}} abla^2 c_{ ext{P}} + k_c \, c_{ ext{Red}} \]

And in a pseudo-first-order catalytic EC' mechanism where \( ext{Red}\) regenerates \( ext{Ox}\) at rate \(k_{ ext{cat}} c_{ ext{Red}}\):

\[ rac{\partial c_{ ext{Ox}}}{\partial t} = D_{ ext{Ox}} abla^2 c_{ ext{Ox}} + k_{ ext{cat}} \, c_{ ext{Red}}, \qquad rac{\partial c_{ ext{Red}}}{\partial t} = D_{ ext{Red}} abla^2 c_{ ext{Red}} - k_{ ext{cat}} \, c_{ ext{Red}} \]

docs.title: Timescale Competition & Stiffness
docs.text:
Just like heterogeneous kinetics, homogeneous chemistry is governed by a dimensionless kinetic parameter comparing the chemical rate \(k_c\) to the experimental timescale \(t_{\exp}\) (in CV, \(t_{\exp} \sim \frac{R T}{n F v}\)):

\[ \lambda = k_c \, t_{\exp} = \frac{k_c R T}{n F v} \]
  • Slow chemistry (\(\lambda \ll 1\)): \(\text{Red}\) diffuses away before reacting; the response resembles a simple E mechanism.
  • Fast chemistry (\(\lambda \gg 1\)): \(\text{Red}\) is consumed within a thin reaction–diffusion layer of thickness \(\mu = \sqrt{D / k_c} \ll \delta\) near the electrode.

Numerical Stiffness & Grid Resolution

When \(k_c\) is large (\(\lambda \gg 1\)), the reaction layer \(\mu = \sqrt{D / k_c}\) can be orders of magnitude thinner than the diffusion layer \(\delta = 6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}\). Use a stretched mesh (GeometricExpandingMesh or ExponentialMesh) to resolve \(\mu\) near \(x = 0\), and use an implicit or stiff solver ("scipy_ivp" with "Radau"/"BDF", "implicit", or "crank_nicolson") rather than an explicit solver. ReactionNetwork and Mechanism automatically supply analytical Jacobians to ScipyIVPSolver for fast, stable stiff integration.

docs.title: Mass Transport
docs.text: Once an electron transfers at the electrode surface, reactant is depleted and product accumulates. How quickly fresh reactant arrives—and product leaves—is governed by mass transport. In Soft Potato, mass transport is modelled in 1D across multiple electrode geometries (PlanarGeometry, SphericalGeometry, CylindricalGeometry) and hydrodynamic convection (RotatingDiskElectrode).

docs.title: Fick's Laws of Diffusion
docs.text:
In an unstirred (quiescent) solution with excess supporting electrolyte (so migration is negligible), mass transport is purely diffusive.

  • Fick's First Law relates the molar flux \(J\) (\(\text{mol}\,\text{m}^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)) to the concentration gradient:

$$ J = -D \frac{\partial c}{\partial x} $$

At the electrode surface (\(x = 0\)), the Faradaic current is directly proportional to this interfacial gradient:

$$ I(t) = n F A \, D \left.\frac{\partial c_{\text{Ox}}}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} $$

  • Fick's Second Law describes how concentration evolves over time in a general 1D radial/planar coordinate \(r\):

$$ \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 c = D \left( \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial r^2} + \frac{p}{r} \frac{\partial c}{\partial r} \right) $$

where \(p\) is the geometric dimensionality index.

docs.title: Electrode Geometries
docs.text:
Soft Potato unifies planar, cylindrical, and spherical diffusion through the geometry parameter \(p\):

Geometry Soft Potato Class Index \(p\) Coordinate \(r\) Physical Regime & Current Behavior Planar PlanarGeometry(area=...) \(0\) \(x \ge 0\) Linear semi-infinite diffusion. Diffusion layer grows as \(\delta \sim \sqrt{D t}\); step current decays as \(t^{-1/2}\) (Cottrell) and never reaches a non-zero steady state. Cylindrical CylindricalGeometry(r0=..., length=...) \(1\) \(r \ge r_0\) Radial diffusion to a wire/fiber microelectrode. Quasi-steady state at long times (\(t \gg r_0^2 / D\)) with logarithmic decay. Spherical / Hemispherical SphericalGeometry(r0=..., hemisphere=...) \(2\) \(r \ge r_0\) Convergent radial diffusion. Reaches a true non-zero steady-state current at long times because spherical shells expand faster than the depletion zone.

docs.title: Planar vs. Spherical & Microelectrode Diffusion
docs.text:
At a macroelectrode (\(r_0 \gg \sqrt{D t}\)), edge effects are negligible and diffusion is effectively planar (\(p = 0\)). Under a potential step to the mass-transport limit, the current follows the Cottrell equation:

\[ I(t) = \frac{n F A D^{1/2} c^*}{\sqrt{\pi t}} \]

At a microelectrode (ultramicroelectrode, UME, typically \(r_0 \le 25\,\mu\text{m}\)), the diffusion layer quickly exceeds the electrode radius (\(\sqrt{D t} \gg r_0\)). Radial (convergent) diffusion dominates, producing a steady-state limiting current:

  • Hemisphere (\(A = 2\pi r_0^2\)): \(I_{\text{ss}} = 2 \pi n F D c^* r_0\)
  • Full sphere (\(A = 4\pi r_0^2\)): \(I_{\text{ss}} = 4 \pi n F D c^* r_0\)
  • Microdisc (inlaid disk of radius \(a\), analytical model in softpotato.analytical.microelectrodes): \(I_{\text{ss}} = 4 n F D c^* a\)

In cyclic voltammetry, this transition from planar to convergent diffusion transforms a peak-shaped voltammogram (at fast scan rates or large electrodes) into a sigmoidal steady-state wave (at slow scan rates or microelectrodes).

docs.title: Rotating Disk Electrode (RDE) Convection–Diffusion
docs.text:
When a disk electrode rotates at angular velocity \(\omega\) (\( ext{rad/s}\)), centrifugal force flings solution outward radially and draws fresh bulk solution axially toward the disk. Near the surface, the von Kármán axial velocity is:

\[ v_x(x) = -0.51023\,\omega^{3/2} u^{-1/2} x^2 \]

where \( u\) is the electrolyte kinematic viscosity (\(\approx 10^{-6} ext{ m}^2/ ext{s}\) for water at \(298 ext{ K}\)).

Soft Potato's RotatingDiskElectrode supports two hydrodynamic descriptions:

  1. Nernst Diffusion Layer (model="nernst_layer", default): Approximates forced convection by truncating pure diffusion at a fixed Nernst diffusion layer thickness \(\delta_N\), where bulk concentration is held constant (\(c(\delta_N, t) = c^*\)):

$$ \delta_N = 1.610 \, D^{1/3} u^{1/6} \omega^{-1/2} $$

  1. Full Convective–Diffusion (model="convective_diffusion"): Solves the full 1D axial advection–diffusion PDE on an extended domain \(x \in [0, k \delta_N]\) (default \(k = 3.0\)):

$$ rac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D rac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2} - v_x(x) rac{\partial c}{\partial x} $$

Both models recover the Levich equation for the mass-transport-limited plateau current:

\[ I_L = 0.620 \, n F A D^{2/3} u^{-1/6} c^* \omega^{1/2} \]

When interfacial kinetics are also finite, the total current obeys the Koutecký–Levich relation:

\[ rac{1}{I} = rac{1}{I_K} + rac{1}{I_L} = rac{1}{I_K} + rac{1}{B \, \omega^{1/2}} \]

allowing kinetic current \(I_K\) and diffusivity \(D\) to be separated cleanly by varying \(\omega\).

docs.title: Benchmarking & Validation
docs.text: A numerical simulation is only trustworthy once it has been verified against known exact mathematics. Soft Potato includes an automated validation suite in softpotato.analytical.benchmark that compares numerical PDE solvers (softpotato.solver) against closed-form analytical solutions (softpotato.analytical).

docs.title: Error Norms (BenchmarkMetrics)
docs.text:
Given a numerical array \(u^{\text{num}}\) and an analytical reference \(u^{\text{exact}}\) over \(N\) points, compute_error_metrics reports:

Metric Formula What It Captures RMSE \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (u_i^{\text{num}} - u_i^{\text{exact}})^2}\) Overall root-mean-square deviation in physical units. Max Absolute Error (\(L_\infty\)) \(\max_i \lvert u_i^{\text{num}} - u_i^{\text{exact}} \rvert\) Worst-case pointwise error (often at \(x = 0\) or sharp fronts). Relative \(L_2\) Error \(\frac{\lVert u^{\text{num}} - u^{\text{exact}} \rVert_2}{\lVert u^{\text{exact}} \rVert_2}\) Scale-independent global accuracy across the entire profile or transient. MAE / MRE Mean absolute & mean relative error Average pointwise accuracy with zero-division protection.

docs.title: Order-of-Convergence Verification
docs.text:
For a well-posed discretization of order \(p\), halving the spatial step \(\Delta x\) or time step \(\Delta t\) should reduce the error by a factor of \(2^p\):

\[ \text{Error}(h) \approx C \, h^p \implies \log(\text{Error}) \approx \log C + p \log h \]

Soft Potato automates this check via estimate_convergence_order, verify_spatial_convergence, and verify_temporal_convergence:

  • Spatial convergence: All built-in finite-difference stencils should observe \(p \approx 2\) (\(\mathcal{O}(\Delta x^2)\)) on uniform grids.
  • Temporal convergence: ImplicitFiniteDifference (BTCS) should observe \(p \approx 1\) (\(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)\)), while CrankNicolson should observe \(p \approx 2\) (\(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2)\)).

docs.title: Canonical Electrochemical Benchmarks
docs.text:
softpotato.analytical.benchmark ships with five canonical benchmark problems, executable individually via run_benchmark() or all together via run_benchmark_suite():

Benchmark Function / Case Analytical Reference What It Validates run_fourier_decay_benchmark 1D sine-mode decay \(c(x,t) = \sin(\pi x / L)\exp(-D\pi^2 t / L^2)\) Interior diffusion operator and pure spatial/temporal accuracy without boundary singularities. run_cottrell_benchmark Planar Cottrell profile \(c(x,t) = c^*\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{D t}}\right)\) & Cottrell current Surface flux extraction, boundary-layer resolution, and step-edge handling. run_spherical_cottrell_benchmark Spherical Cottrell transient & radial profile Radial \(p = 2\) spherical Laplacian \(\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial r^2} + \frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial c}{\partial r}\) and steady-state convergence. run_mass_conservation_benchmark Constant total integral \(\int c(x,t)\,dx = \text{const}\) Zero-flux Neumann boundary conditions and discrete mass conservation. run_grid_efficiency_benchmark Planar Cottrell on Uniform1DMesh vs. GeometricExpandingMesh vs. ExponentialMesh Accuracy vs. node count, runtime speedup, and memory scaling of stretched grids.

docs.title: Spatial Grids & Meshes
docs.text: To solve Fick's second law numerically, Soft Potato replaces the continuous spatial coordinate \(x \in [x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\) with a discrete 1D mesh of \(N\) nodes \(x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{N-1}\). How those nodes are spaced determines both numerical accuracy and computational speed.

docs.title: Sizing the Domain: The Diffusion Layer
docs.text:
In semi-infinite planar diffusion, concentration perturbations spread outward from the electrode (\(x = 0\)) over a characteristic distance \(\sim \sqrt{D t}\). From the exact error-function solution for a potential step, at \(x = 6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}\):

\[ \operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}}{2\sqrt{D t_{\max}}}\right) = \operatorname{erfc}(3) \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-5} \]

Setting the outer domain boundary to \(\delta = 6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}\) guarantees that the bulk concentration remains undisturbed (\(c(x_{\max}, t) \approx c^*\)) to within \(0.002\%\), without wasting grid points far out in the bulk solution.

Soft Potato automates this calculation via create_diffusion_mesh(D, t_max, factor=6.0, kind=...) (and diffusion_layer_thickness).

When the Domain Is Fixed Physically

For a Rotating Disk Electrode (model="nernst_layer"), the outer boundary is instead set by the hydrodynamic Nernst diffusion layer \(\delta_N = 1.610\,D^{1/3}\nu^{1/6}\omega^{-1/2}\) (or \(k \delta_N\) for "convective_diffusion"). See Mass Transport.

docs.title: Boundary-Layer Resolution & Non-Uniform Stencils
docs.text:
Near \(x = 0\), concentration gradients \(\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0}\) are steepest—especially right after a potential step (\(t \to 0^+\)) or inside a fast homogeneous reaction layer \(\mu = \sqrt{D / k_c}\). Far from the electrode, concentration varies smoothly.

  • A uniform grid wastes most of its nodes in the smooth bulk region in order to make \(\Delta x\) small enough at the surface.
  • A stretched (expanding) grid clusters nodes tightly near \(x = 0\) (small \(\Delta x_0\)) and expands smoothly toward \(x_{\max}\), achieving the same surface flux accuracy with 10×–50× fewer nodes.

On any non-uniform grid with local spacings \(h_{j-1} = x_j - x_{j-1}\) and \(h_j = x_{j+1} - x_j\), Soft Potato discretizes the second derivative using the standard 3-point finite-difference stencil:

\[ \left.\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}\right|_{x_j} \approx \frac{2}{h_{j-1} + h_j} \left( \frac{c_{j+1} - c_j}{h_j} - \frac{c_j - c_{j-1}}{h_{j-1}} \right) \]

docs.title: Mesh Comparison: Uniform1DMesh vs. ExponentialMesh vs. GeometricExpandingMesh
docs.text:
Mesh Class create_diffusion_mesh kind Node Spacing Law Key Parameters Best For Uniform1DMesh "uniform" Constant \(\Delta x = \frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{N - 1}\) n_points or dx Smooth interior profiles, Fourier decay benchmarks, and teaching/prototyping. GeometricExpandingMesh "geometric" (default) \(\Delta x_j = \Delta x_0 \, \gamma^j\) (\(\gamma > 1\)) Any two of n_points, gamma, dx_min; two_sided General electrochemistry (CV, CA, RDE, EC/EC' mechanisms). Predictable surface spacing \(\Delta x_0\) and smooth geometric growth. ExponentialMesh "exponential" Smooth coordinate mapping ("exponential", "tanh", "sinh") n_points, stretching beta (\(\beta > 0\)), mapping, two_sided High-order smooth stretching across \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\) or symmetric two-electrode cells (two_sided=True).

CFL Penalty on Fine Surface Grids

Clustered meshes have a very small \(\Delta x_0\) at the electrode. Because explicit time-stepping requires \(\Delta t \le \frac{\Delta x_{\min}^2}{2 D}\), never pair a tightly clustered expanding mesh with an explicit solver—use an implicit or adaptive solver ("scipy_ivp", "crank_nicolson", or "implicit").

docs.title: Time-Stepping & Solvers
docs.text:
Once space is discretized onto a 1D mesh, the reaction–diffusion PDE becomes a coupled system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in time—one equation per species per interior grid node:

\[ \frac{d\mathbf{c}}{dt} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{c}, t) + \mathbf{b}(t) \]

where \(\mathbf{L}\) is the discrete diffusion/advection operator, \(\mathbf{R}\) is the homogeneous reaction term, and \(\mathbf{b}(t)\) encodes the electrode and bulk boundary conditions. Soft Potato provides four built-in solvers in softpotato.solver.

docs.title: 1. Explicit Finite Difference (ExplicitFiniteDifference, "explicit" / "ftcs")
docs.text:
Uses Forward-Time Central-Space (FTCS): the future state \(\mathbf{c}^{n+1}\) is computed directly from the current state \(\mathbf{c}^n\):

\[ \frac{\mathbf{c}^{n+1} - \mathbf{c}^n}{\Delta t} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{c}^n + \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{c}^n, t_n) \]
  • Accuracy: \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t, \Delta x^2)\).
  • Stability: Conditionally stable. Diffusion requires the CFL (Fourier) condition:

$$ \text{Fo} = \frac{D \Delta t}{\Delta x_{\min}^2} \le \frac{1}{2} $$

If \(\Delta t\) violates this bound, numerical oscillations blow up exponentially. Soft Potato enforces this stability check automatically.

docs.title: 2. Implicit Finite Difference (ImplicitFiniteDifference, "implicit" / "btcs")
docs.text:
Uses Backward-Time Central-Space (BTCS) (backward Euler), evaluating the right-hand side at the unknown next step \(t_{n+1}\):

\[ \frac{\mathbf{c}^{n+1} - \mathbf{c}^n}{\Delta t} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{c}^{n+1} + \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{c}^{n+1}, t_{n+1}) \]
  • Accuracy: \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t, \Delta x^2)\) (first-order in time).
  • Stability: Unconditionally stable and L-stable—it strongly damps high-frequency spatial noise, making it ideal right after sharp potential steps.

docs.title: 3. Crank–Nicolson (CrankNicolson, "crank_nicolson" / "crank-nicolson")
docs.text:
Averages the explicit and implicit operators at \(t_n\) and \(t_{n+1}\) (trapezoidal rule in time):

\[ \frac{\mathbf{c}^{n+1} - \mathbf{c}^n}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\mathbf{L}\mathbf{c}^n + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{c}^{n+1}\right] + \dots \]
  • Accuracy: \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2, \Delta x^2)\) (second-order in both space and time).
  • Stability: Unconditionally stable (A-stable), though not L-stable: very large time steps across a discontinuous step change can introduce mild ringing near \(x = 0\) unless \(\Delta t\) is kept moderate.

docs.title: 4. Method of Lines (ScipyIVPSolver, "scipy_ivp" / "solve_ivp")
docs.text:
Passes the semi-discrete ODE system to scipy.integrate.solve_ivp with adaptive time-stepping and automatic error control (rtol, atol).

  • Supported integrators: Implicit stiff solvers ("BDF", "Radau") and explicit Runge–Kutta ("RK45", "DOP853").
  • Why it is the default in simulate(): Electrochemical diffusion on stretched meshes is stiff (eigenvalues span many orders of magnitude between \(\Delta x_0\) and \(\Delta x_{\max}\)), and homogeneous reactions add further stiffness. "Radau" / "BDF" automatically take tiny steps right after a potential jump and large steps once the profile smooths out, using sparse/analytical Jacobians from ReactionNetwork and Mechanism.

docs.title: Solver Comparison
docs.text: Solver Registry Names Time Order Stability Best Use Case ScipyIVPSolver "scipy_ivp", "solve_ivp" Adaptive (up to 5th order) Stiff-stable (Radau / BDF) Default choice for CV, CA, pulse, RDE, and stiff EC/EC' mechanisms on expanding grids. CrankNicolson "crank_nicolson", "crank-nicolson" \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^2)\) Unconditionally stable Fixed-step high-accuracy diffusion benchmarks and smooth waveforms. ImplicitFiniteDifference "implicit", "btcs" \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)\) Unconditionally stable (L-stable) Step-edge robustness when damping high-frequency transients matters more than 2nd-order time accuracy. ExplicitFiniteDifference "explicit", "ftcs" \(\mathcal{O}(\Delta t)\) \(\Delta t \le \frac{\Delta x_{\min}^2}{2 D}\) Pedagogical comparisons and uniform grids with small \(\Delta t\).

docs.title: Step-Edge Events & Piecewise Integration
docs.text:
Electrochemical waveforms frequently contain discontinuities or slope kinks:

  • Potential steps (Chronoamperometry, SampledCurrentVoltammetry, DifferentialPulseVoltammetry, SquareWaveVoltammetry): instantaneous jumps in \(E(t)\).
  • Switching vertices (CyclicVoltammetry): sudden reversal of \(dE/dt\) from \(-v\) to \(+v\).
  • Multi-segment waveforms (CustomWaveform): transitions between ConstantSegment, LinearRampSegment, etc.

If an adaptive ODE solver integrates blindly across a discontinuity, it either wastes steps hunting for the jump or smears the vertex. Every technique in softpotato.techniques therefore exposes its exact interior discontinuity timestamps via technique.event_times.

During simulate(), Soft Potato partitions \([0, t_{\text{end}}]\) at event_times into smooth sub-intervals \([t_k, t_{k+1}]\), integrating each sub-interval cleanly and restarting the solver at each event with the exact concentration state.

docs.title: Recipe: Analytical Baselines
docs.text:
Compute exact theoretical baselines for Cottrell (chronoamperometry), Levich (RDE), Randles–Ševčík (CV peak currents), and SECM approach curves—with zero PDEs or meshes.

Edit only the physical parameters (n, D, c_bulk, area, nu, T, RG, kappa) at the top of the script.

docs.title: Full Runnable Script
docs.text:
"""5-Minute Analytical Baselines: Cottrell, Levich, Randles-Sevcik, and SECM.

Edit only the physical parameters in the CONFIGURATION section below to compute
exact theoretical currents and approach curves without setting up any PDEs or meshes.
"""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from softpotato import analytical as spa

# ==============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION — Edit physical parameters here
# ==============================================================================
n = 1  # Number of electrons transferred
D = 6.7e-6  # Diffusion coefficient [cm^2/s] (e.g. ferrocyanide in water)
c_bulk = 1.0e-6  # Bulk concentration [mol/cm^3] (1.0e-6 mol/cm^3 = 1.0 mM)
area = 0.0707  # Electrode area [cm^2] (3 mm diameter disk)
nu = 0.01  # Kinematic viscosity [cm^2/s] (aqueous ~ 0.01 cm^2/s)
T = 298.15  # Temperature [K]

# SECM tip geometry & kinetics
RG = 5.0  # Insulator-to-electrode radius ratio (r_g / a)
kappa = 2.0  # Dimensionless substrate rate constant (k * a / D)

# ==============================================================================
# 1. Cottrell Equation (Chronoamperometry)
# ==============================================================================
t = np.linspace(0.05, 5.0, 200)  # Time after step [s]
i_cottrell = spa.cottrell(t, n=n, D=D, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area)

# ==============================================================================
# 2. Levich Equation (Rotating Disk Electrode)
# ==============================================================================
rpm = np.linspace(100, 2500, 100)  # Rotation rate [rpm]
i_levich = spa.levich(rpm=rpm, n=n, D=D, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area, nu=nu)

# ==============================================================================
# 3. Randles-Sevcik Equation (Cyclic Voltammetry Peak Current)
# ==============================================================================
v = np.linspace(0.01, 1.0, 100)  # Scan rate [V/s]
i_peak = spa.randles_sevcik(v, c_bulk=c_bulk, D=D, area=area, n=n, T=T)

# ==============================================================================
# 4. SECM Approach Curves (Conducting, Insulating, and Finite Kinetics)
# ==============================================================================
L = np.linspace(0.15, 5.0, 200)  # Normalized tip-substrate distance (d / a)
i_cond = spa.secm_approach_positive_feedback(L, RG=RG)
i_ins = spa.secm_approach_negative_feedback(L, RG=RG)
i_kin = spa.secm_approach_curve(L, RG=RG, kappa=kappa)

# ==============================================================================
# Print Summary & Plot
# ==============================================================================
print(
    f"Cottrell current at t = 1.0 s:    {spa.cottrell(1.0, n=n, D=D, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area) * 1e6:.2f} uA"
)
print(
    f"Levich current at 1600 rpm:       {spa.levich(rpm=1600, n=n, D=D, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area, nu=nu) * 1e6:.2f} uA"
)
print(
    f"Randles-Sevcik peak at 0.1 V/s:   {spa.randles_sevcik(0.1, c_bulk=c_bulk, D=D, area=area, n=n, T=T) * 1e6:.2f} uA"
)
print(
    f"SECM finite-kinetics at L = 0.5:  {spa.secm_approach_curve(0.5, RG=RG, kappa=kappa):.3f} (normalized)"
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 7.5))

axes[0, 0].plot(t, i_cottrell * 1e6)
axes[0, 0].set(title="Cottrell Transient", xlabel="Time / s", ylabel="Current / uA")
axes[0, 0].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[0, 1].plot(rpm, i_levich * 1e6)
axes[0, 1].set(
    title="Levich Limiting Current",
    xlabel="Rotation Rate / rpm",
    ylabel="Limiting Current / uA",
)
axes[0, 1].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[1, 0].plot(np.sqrt(v), i_peak * 1e6)
axes[1, 0].set(
    title="Randles-Sevcik Peak Current",
    xlabel=r"$v^{1/2}$ / $(V/s)^{1/2}$",
    ylabel="Peak Current / uA",
)
axes[1, 0].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[1, 1].plot(L, i_cond, label="Conducting (pos. feedback)")
axes[1, 1].plot(L, i_kin, label=f"Kinetic (kappa={kappa})")
axes[1, 1].plot(L, i_ins, label="Insulating (neg. feedback)")
axes[1, 1].set(
    title=f"SECM Approach Curves (RG={RG})",
    xlabel="Normalized Distance L = d/a",
    ylabel="Normalized Current $I_T$",
)
axes[1, 1].legend()
axes[1, 1].grid(alpha=0.3)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Save the code above as recipe_analytical.py and run:

python recipe_analytical.py

Units Reminder

In softpotato.analytical, keep length units consistent across D, area, nu, and c_bulk: if D is in \(\text{cm}^2/\text{s}\) and area is in \(\text{cm}^2\), pass c_bulk in \(\text{mol}/\text{cm}^3\) (\(1\text{ mM} = 10^{-6}\text{ mol}/\text{cm}^3\)) so the returned current is in Amperes (\(\text{A}\)).

docs.title: Recipe: First Simulation (Cyclic Voltammetry)
docs.text:
Run a complete Butler–Volmer cyclic voltammetry simulation and plot the resulting voltammogram in a single simulate() + plot_result() call. Soft Potato automatically constructs a physics-informed spatial mesh and solves the reaction–diffusion PDE for you.

Edit only the physical parameters (E0, D, c_bulk, k0, alpha, area) and waveform parameters (E_start, E_vertex1, E_vertex2, v) at the top of the script. Passing PlanarGeometry(area) to simulate() scales the Faradaic current to the electrode area in Amperes (\(\text{A}\)).

docs.title: Full Runnable Script
docs.text:
"""5-Minute First Simulation: Cyclic Voltammetry with simulate() and plot_result().

Edit only the physical and waveform parameters below to simulate a cyclic
voltammogram and plot it in one call—no manual mesh or PDE setup required.
"""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from softpotato.geometry import PlanarGeometry
from softpotato.reactions import ButlerVolmer, Species
from softpotato.techniques import CyclicVoltammetry, plot_result, simulate

# ==============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION — Edit physical & waveform parameters here
# ==============================================================================
# Redox couple & electrode parameters (SI units: m^2/s, mol/m^3 = mM, m^2)
E0 = 0.0  # Formal potential [V]
D = 1.0e-9  # Diffusion coefficient [m^2/s] (= 1.0e-5 cm^2/s)
c_bulk = 1.0  # Bulk concentration of Ox [mol/m^3] (= 1.0 mM)
k0 = 1.0e-3  # Heterogeneous rate constant [m/s] (= 0.1 cm/s)
alpha = 0.5  # Transfer coefficient [-]
area = 7.07e-6  # Electrode area [m^2] (= 0.0707 cm^2, 3 mm disk)

# Cyclic voltammetry waveform
E_start = 0.4  # Initial potential [V]
E_vertex1 = -0.4  # First switching potential [V]
E_vertex2 = 0.4  # Second switching potential [V]
v = 0.1  # Scan rate [V/s]

# ==============================================================================
# Run Simulation & Plot
# ==============================================================================
ox = Species(
    "Ox", diffusivity=D, bulk_concentration=c_bulk, standard_potential=E0, n_electrons=1
)
red = Species("Red", diffusivity=D, bulk_concentration=0.0)

cv = CyclicVoltammetry(
    E_start=E_start, E_vertex1=E_vertex1, E_vertex2=E_vertex2, scan_rate=v
)
kinetics = ButlerVolmer(k0=k0, alpha=alpha, E0=E0, n=1)
geometry = PlanarGeometry(area)

# Species must be ordered [ox, red] according to the reduction reaction: Ox + e- -> Red
result = simulate(cv, [ox, red], geometry=geometry, kinetics=kinetics)

print(f"Simulated {len(result.time)} time points over {result.time[-1]:.2f} s")
print(f"Peak cathodic current: {result.current.min() * 1e6:.2f} uA")
print(f"Peak anodic current:   {result.current.max() * 1e6:.2f} uA")

fig, ax = plot_result(result)
ax.set_title(f"Cyclic Voltammogram (v = {v} V/s, k0 = {k0:.1e} m/s)")
plt.show()

Species Ordering ([ox, red])

When passing a list of species directly to simulate(), the list must be ordered [ox, red] according to the reduction reaction \(\text{Ox} + e^- \rightarrow \text{Red}\) (oxidized species first, reduced species second).

docs.title: What simulate() Returns
docs.text:
result is a TechniqueResult object containing:

  • result.time — time array (\(\text{s}\))
  • result.potential — applied potential (\(\text{V}\))
  • result.current — simulated Faradaic current (\(\text{A}\))
  • result["Ox"] and result["Red"] — spatial concentration profiles

Pass result directly to plot_result(result) for an instant publication-ready figure.

docs.title: Recipe: Fitting Experimental Data
docs.text:
Extract physical and geometric parameters—with \(R^2\) and 95% confidence intervals—from chronoamperometry, cyclic voltammetry, and SECM measurements using softpotato.analytical.fitting:

  • fit_cottrell() → extracts diffusion coefficient \(D\)
  • fit_randles_sevcik() → extracts diffusion coefficient \(D\) from \(I_p\) vs. \(v\)
  • fit_secm_approach() → extracts tip insulator ratio \(RG\) and zero-distance offset \(d_{\text{offset}}\)

docs.title: Full Runnable Script
docs.text:
"""5-Minute Experimental Data Fitting: Cottrell, Randles-Sevcik, and SECM.

Demonstrates how to extract physical parameters (D, RG, d_offset) with R^2
and 95% confidence intervals using softpotato.analytical.fitting.
Replace the synthetic arrays below with your own experimental measurements.
"""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from softpotato import analytical as spa

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ==============================================================================
# KNOWN EXPERIMENTAL CONSTANTS — Edit to match your cell
# ==============================================================================
n = 1  # Electrons transferred
c_bulk = 1.0e-6  # Bulk concentration [mol/cm^3] (1.0 mM)
area = 0.0707  # Macroelectrode area [cm^2]
T = 298.15  # Temperature [K]
a_ume = 12.5e-6  # SECM UME radius [m] (25 um diameter)

# ==============================================================================
# 1. Fit Cottrell Chronoamperometry -> Extract D
# ==============================================================================
t_exp = np.linspace(0.05, 4.0, 80)
i_true_ca = spa.cottrell(t_exp, n=n, D=6.7e-6, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area)
i_exp_ca = i_true_ca + rng.normal(0.0, 2.5e-7, size=t_exp.size)

ca_fit = spa.fit_cottrell(
    t_exp,
    i_exp_ca,
    n=n,
    area=area,
    c_bulk=c_bulk,
    confidence_level=0.95,
)
ci_d_ca = ca_fit.confidence_intervals["D"]
print("=== Cottrell Fit ===")
print(
    f"  D      = {ca_fit.d:.3e} cm^2/s  (95% CI: [{ci_d_ca[0]:.3e}, {ci_d_ca[1]:.3e}])"
)
print(f"  R^2    = {ca_fit.r_squared:.5f}")

# ==============================================================================
# 2. Fit Randles-Sevcik Peak Currents -> Extract D
# ==============================================================================
v_exp = np.array([0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0])
ip_true = spa.randles_sevcik(v_exp, c_bulk=c_bulk, D=6.7e-6, area=area, n=n, T=T)
ip_exp = ip_true + rng.normal(0.0, 1.2e-6, size=v_exp.size)

rs_fit = spa.fit_randles_sevcik(
    v_exp,
    ip_exp,
    n=n,
    area=area,
    c_bulk=c_bulk,
    T=T,
    confidence_level=0.95,
)
ci_d_rs = rs_fit.confidence_intervals["D"]
print("\n=== Randles-Sevcik Fit ===")
print(
    f"  D      = {rs_fit.d:.3e} cm^2/s  (95% CI: [{ci_d_rs[0]:.3e}, {ci_d_rs[1]:.3e}])"
)
print(f"  R^2    = {rs_fit.r_squared:.5f}")

# ==============================================================================
# 3. Fit SECM Approach Curve -> Extract RG and d_offset
# ==============================================================================
d_exp = np.linspace(3.0e-6, 50.0e-6, 60)
L_true = (d_exp - 0.8e-6) / a_ume
it_true = spa.secm_approach_positive_feedback(L_true, RG=5.2)
it_exp = it_true + rng.normal(0.0, 0.03, size=d_exp.size)

secm_fit = spa.fit_secm_approach(
    d_exp,
    it_exp,
    substrate="conducting",
    a=a_ume,
    confidence_level=0.95,
)
ci_rg = secm_fit.confidence_intervals["rg"]
ci_d0 = secm_fit.confidence_intervals["d_offset"]
print("\n=== SECM Approach Fit ===")
print(f"  RG       = {secm_fit.rg:.2f}  (95% CI: [{ci_rg[0]:.2f}, {ci_rg[1]:.2f}])")
print(
    f"  d_offset = {secm_fit.d_offset * 1e6:.2f} um  (95% CI: [{ci_d0[0] * 1e6:.2f}, {ci_d0[1] * 1e6:.2f}] um)"
)
print(f"  R^2      = {secm_fit.r_squared:.5f}")

# ==============================================================================
# Plot Data vs. Fits
# ==============================================================================
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4))

axes[0].scatter(t_exp, i_exp_ca * 1e6, s=16, alpha=0.7, label="Data")
axes[0].plot(
    t_exp,
    ca_fit.y_fit * 1e6,
    color="C1",
    lw=2,
    label=f"Fit ($R^2={ca_fit.r_squared:.4f}$)",
)
axes[0].set(title="Cottrell Fit", xlabel="Time / s", ylabel="Current / uA")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[1].scatter(np.sqrt(v_exp), ip_exp * 1e6, s=28, alpha=0.8, label="Data")
axes[1].plot(
    np.sqrt(v_exp),
    rs_fit.y_fit * 1e6,
    color="C1",
    lw=2,
    label=f"Fit ($R^2={rs_fit.r_squared:.4f}$)",
)
axes[1].set(
    title="Randles-Sevcik Fit",
    xlabel=r"$v^{1/2}$ / $(V/s)^{1/2}$",
    ylabel="Peak Current / uA",
)
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

axes[2].scatter(d_exp * 1e6, it_exp, s=16, alpha=0.7, label="Data")
axes[2].plot(
    d_exp * 1e6,
    secm_fit.y_fit,
    color="C1",
    lw=2,
    label=f"Fit ($R^2={secm_fit.r_squared:.4f}$)",
)
axes[2].set(
    title="SECM Approach Fit",
    xlabel="Stage Position d / um",
    ylabel="Normalized Current $I_T$",
)
axes[2].legend()
axes[2].grid(alpha=0.3)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.text:
Soft Potato is organized in layers—from one-line closed-form equations up to custom multi-species PDE solvers. Pick the row that matches what you want to do:

If you want to… Use Typical inputs Where to go next Compute an exact theoretical baseline (Cottrell, Randles–Ševčík, Levich, Butler–Volmer, microelectrodes, SECM) softpotato.analytical Physical constants (\(D\), \(c^*\), \(n\), \(A\), \(v\), \(\omega\)) User Guide · API Reference Extract \(D\), \(k^0\), \(\alpha\), or \(RG\) from experimental data with confidence intervals and \(R^2\) softpotato.analytical.fitting Experimental arrays (t, i, E, v, omega) User Guide · API Reference Simulate a standard electrochemical experiment (CA, LSV, CV, SCV, DPV, SWV, CP, RDE) with automatic plotting and diagnostics softpotato.techniques.simulate() Waveform object (e.g. CyclicVoltammetry(...)) + physical parameters User Guide · Tutorials Build a custom reaction–diffusion model with bespoke grids, geometries, boundary conditions, or PDE solvers softpotato.solver.DiffusionProblem() Spatial grid (grid), diffusivity, boundary_conditions, initial_conditions, reactions / mechanism Concepts · Tutorials

Chip's Tip

If you are unsure where to start, begin with softpotato.analytical for quick reference curves or softpotato.techniques.simulate() for full voltammetric and transient simulations. Drop down to DiffusionProblem() only when you need custom meshes, non-standard boundary conditions, or custom solver settings.

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Model a pseudo-first-order catalytic EC' mechanism ($\text{Ox} + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}$, $\text{Red} \xrightarrow{k_{\text{cat}}} \text{Ox}$) using CatalyticReaction and verify the transition from a peaked CV to a sigmoidal catalytic plateau $I_{\text{cat}} = -n F A c^* \sqrt{D k_{\text{cat}}}$.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text: We couple a fast reversible-limit ButlerVolmer step ($k^0 = 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}$) with CatalyticReaction(red, ox, k=k_cat) across $k_{\text{cat}} \in \{0, 0.5, 2.0, 10.0\}\text{ s}^{-1}$.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We simulate each k_cat using solver="scipy_ivp".

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We overlay the catalytic CVs and compare the plateau current at $-0.4\text{ V}$ against the analytical steady-state catalytic limit $I_{\text{cat}} = -n F A c^* \sqrt{D k_{\text{cat}}}$.

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Regenerating $\text{Ox}$ in solution sustains a steady-state reaction–diffusion layer of thickness $\mu = \sqrt{D / k_{\text{cat}}}$.
  • At large $k_{\text{cat}}$, the reverse peak disappears and the forward wave becomes a scan-rate-independent sigmoidal plateau with $I_{\text{cat}} = -n F A c^* \sqrt{D k_{\text{cat}}}$.
  • Next: Read Reaction Mechanisms Concepts.

nich = analyze_nicholson(cv_results[3.0e-5], D=D, n=1)
print(f"Nicholson (true k0 = 3.00e-5 m/s):")
print(f"  delta_Ep = {nich.delta_Ep_mv:.1f} mV, Psi = {nich.psi:.3f}, k0 = {nich.k0:.2e} m/s, regime = {nich.regime!r}")

tafel_fit = analyze_tafel(

)
print(f"Tafel (true alpha = 0.50, k0 = 1.00e-7 m/s):")
print(f"  alpha = {tafel_fit.alpha:.3f}, k0 = {tafel_fit.k0:.2e} m/s, slope = {tafel_fit.slope_mv:.1f} mV/dec")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.2))
for k0, res in cv_results.items():
    axes[0].plot(res.potential, res.current * 1e6, lw=1.8, label=f"$k^0 = {k0:.0e}$ m/s")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Potential $E$ [V]")

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Explore the transition from reversible to quasi-reversible and irreversible CV as $k^0$ decreases, extract $k^0$ via Nicholson's method (analyze_nicholson()), and extract $\alpha$ and $k^0$ in the irreversible regime via analyze_tafel().

docs.text: We simulate CVs across the four $k^0$ values and an LSV at $k^0 = 10^{-6}\text{ m/s}$ for Tafel analysis.

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• High $k^0$ ($\Lambda \gg 10$) gives reversible Nernstian peaks ($\Delta E_p \approx 57\text{ mV}$).

  • Low $k^0$ shifts the wave to large overpotentials where analyze_tafel() extracts $\alpha$ and $k^0$ from $\log_{10}|I|$ vs. $\eta$.

docs.title: The EC Mechanism: Coupled Follow-Up Chemical Reaction¶
1. Goal¶
docs.text: Model an EC mechanism ($\text{Ox} + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}$, $\text{Red} \xrightarrow{k_c} \text{P}$) using Mechanism, ElectrochemicalStep, and FirstOrderReaction, and observe how increasing $k_c$ diminishes the reverse anodic peak.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text: We define three species (Ox, Red, P) and couple a fast reversible-limit ButlerVolmer step ($k^0 = 10^{-2}\text{ m/s}$) with a homogeneous FirstOrderReaction(red, P, k=k_c). The dimensionless kinetic parameter is $\lambda = k_c RT / (n F v)$.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We construct a Mechanism for each $k_c$ and integrate with solver="scipy_ivp" (stiff Radau integrator with analytical Jacobian).

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We overlay the CVs and print $|I_{pa}/I_{pc}|$ and $E_{pc}$ as a function of $\lambda = k_c RT / (n F v)$.

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• As $k_c$ (and $\lambda$) increases, $\text{Red}$ is chemically converted to electro-inactive $\text{P}$ before it can be re-oxidized on the reverse scan.
  • The anodic return peak shrinks ($|I_{pa}/I_{pc}| \to 0$) and the forward cathodic peak shifts slightly positive.
  • Next: Explore EE Mechanism or Catalytic EC' Mechanism.

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Model a sequential two-electron transfer (EE mechanism: $\text{A} + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{B}$ at $E_1^0$, $\text{B} + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{C}$ at $E_2^0$) using two ElectrochemicalSteps in Mechanism, and observe how $\Delta E^0 = E_1^0 - E_2^0$ controls wave separation vs. wave merging.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text:
We define species A, B, and C and test three regimes:

  1. $\Delta E^0 = +0.30\text{ V}$ ($E_1^0 = +0.15\text{ V}, E_2^0 = -0.15\text{ V}$): two well-separated 1-$e^-$ waves.
  2. $\Delta E^0 = +0.05\text{ V}$ ($E_1^0 = +0.025\text{ V}, E_2^0 = -0.025\text{ V}$): overlapping waves.
  3. $\Delta E^0 = -0.15\text{ V}$ ($E_1^0 = -0.075\text{ V}, E_2^0 = +0.075\text{ V}$): potential inversion, merging into a single 2-$e^-$ wave.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We build each two-step Mechanism and simulate with solver="scipy_ivp".

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We overlay the three EE voltammograms to compare peak separation and peak height.

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• When $E_1^0 - E_2^0 \gg RT/F$, two distinct 1-$e^-$ waves appear.
  • When $E_2^0 > E_1^0$ (potential inversion), $\text{B}$ is immediately reduced to $\text{C}$ as soon as it forms, producing a single, sharper 2-$e^-$ wave with larger peak current ($\propto n^{3/2}$).
  • Next: Explore Catalytic EC' Mechanism or Reaction Mechanisms Concepts.

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Simulate a diffusion-controlled reversible one-electron transfer (NernstianEquilibrium) at a planar electrode and verify its classic diagnostic signatures: $\Delta E_p \approx 57\text{ mV}$, $E_{1/2} = E^{0\prime}$, $|I_{pa}/I_{pc}| = 1$, and $I_{pc} = I_{\text{Randles-Ševčík}}$.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text: We set $E^{0\prime} = 0.0\text{ V}$, $D_{\text{Ox}} = D_{\text{Red}} = 10^{-9}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}$, $c^* = 1\text{ mM}$, $v = 0.1\text{ V/s}$, and scan from $+0.4\text{ V}$ to $-0.4\text{ V}$ and back.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We run simulate() with NernstianEquilibrium boundary conditions.

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We inspect the peak diagnostics via find_peaks(), compare $I_{pc}$ against spa.randles_sevcik(), and plot the spatial concentration profiles at the switching potential.

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• At 298.15 K, a reversible planar 1-$e^-$ couple exhibits $\Delta E_p \approx 57\text{–}59\text{ mV}$, $E_{1/2} = E^{0\prime}$ (when $D_{\text{Ox}} = D_{\text{Red}}$), and $|I_{pa}/I_{pc}| = 1$.
  • The diffusion layer grows to $\sim 6\sqrt{D t}$ into solution, depleting $\text{Ox}$ near $x = 0$ and generating $\text{Red}$.
  • Next: See how curvature changes the voltammogram in Reversible Spherical CV.

docs.title: Reversible Spherical CV: Macroelectrode to Microelectrode Transition¶
1. Goal¶
docs.text: Demonstrate how decreasing electrode radius $r_0$ in SphericalGeometry transitions a reversible CV from peak-shaped planar diffusion to a hysteresis-free sigmoidal steady-state wave.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text:
The transition is governed by the dimensionless spherical parameter comparing diffusion layer thickness $\sqrt{D RT / (n F v)}$ to electrode radius $r_0$:

  • $r_0 = 10\text{ mm}$: planar-like peak-shaped CV.
  • $r_0 = 100\,\mu\text{m}$: mixed planar/radial diffusion.
  • $r_0 = 10\,\mu\text{m}$: radial steady-state sigmoidal wave.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We simulate the reversible CV at all three spherical radii and normalize by each sphere's area ($4 \pi r_0^2$) or steady-state limiting current.

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We plot the current density $j = I / A$ for each radius and compare the $r_0 = 10\,\mu\text{m}$ plateau against spa.microsphere_limiting_current().

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Large spherical electrodes ($r_0 \gg \sqrt{Dt}$) behave like planar electrodes with peak-shaped CVs.
  • Microspheres ($r_0 \ll \sqrt{Dt}$) achieve steady-state radial mass transport, giving a sigmoidal wave with negligible forward/reverse hysteresis and limiting current $I_{\text{ss}} = -4\pi n F D c^* r_0$.
  • Next: Explore Planar Randles–Ševčík or Mass Transport Concepts.

docs.title: Randles–Ševčík Analysis: Extracting $D$ from Multi-Scan-Rate CV¶
1. Goal¶
docs.text: Verify the Randles–Ševčík scaling law ($I_p \propto v^{1/2}$) across a scan-rate sweep and extract the diffusion coefficient $D$ with 95% confidence intervals using analyze_randles_sevcik() and fit_randles_sevcik().

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text: We simulate a reversible 1-$e^-$ planar CV at six scan rates: $0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0\text{ V/s}$.

docs.title: 3. Simulation¶
docs.text: We run simulate_sweep() across all six scan rates.

docs.title: 4. Diagnostics & Plots¶
docs.text: We run analyze_randles_sevcik() and fit_randles_sevcik() on the cathodic peak currents, and plot both the overlaid voltammograms and the Randles–Ševčík regression.

docs.title: 5. Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• For a reversible planar process, $|I_p| = 0.4463\, n F A c^* \sqrt{\frac{n F D v}{RT}}$ scales linearly with $v^{1/2}$.
  • analyze_randles_sevcik() and fit_randles_sevcik() recover $D$ with $R^2 > 0.9999$.
  • Next: See how finite kinetics affect $\Delta E_p$ in Butler–Volmer Kinetics & Nicholson Analysis.

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Explore softpotato.analytical directly to perform rapid, vectorized parameter sweeps across transient (cottrell), voltammetric (randles_sevcik, nicholson_psi), hydrodynamic (levich, koutecky_levich), microelectrode (microdisc_limiting_current), and interfacial kinetic (butler_volmer) models.

docs.title: 2. Physical Setup¶
docs.text: All functions in softpotato.analytical operate on NumPy scalars or arrays in SI units ($\text{m}$, $\text{s}$, $\text{mol/m}^3$, $\text{A}$, $\text{V}$). We define a shared set of baseline electrochemical parameters for a one-electron redox couple ($n = 1$, $T = 298.15\text{ K}$).

docs.title: 3. Diffusivity Sweep: Cottrell & Randles–Ševčík Scaling¶
docs.text: Both the Cottrell transient current ($I \propto D^{1/2} t^{-1/2}$) and the reversible CV peak current ($I_p \propto D^{1/2} v^{1/2}$) scale with $\sqrt{D}$. Vectorized array broadcasting makes multi-parameter sweeps instantaneous.

docs.title: 4. Hydrodynamic RDE Sweeps: Levich vs. Koutecký–Levich¶
docs.text:
At a rotating disk electrode (RDE), pure mass-transport control follows the Levich equation ($I_L \propto \omega^{1/2}$), whereas mixed kinetic–diffusion control follows the Koutecký–Levich equation:

$$ \frac{1}{I} = \frac{1}{I_k} + \frac{1}{I_L(\omega)} $$

Below we sweep rotation rate $\text{rpm} \in [200, 3600]$ across several kinetic current limits $I_k$.

docs.title: 5. Microelectrode & Butler–Volmer Kinetic Sweeps¶
docs.text: We also compare steady-state microdisc limiting currents ($I_{\text{ss}} = 4 n F D c^* r_0$) across electrode radii and Butler–Volmer current–overpotential curves across transfer coefficients $\alpha$.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Every model in softpotato.analytical accepts NumPy arrays in SI units for instant vectorized parameter sweeps.
  • Combining levich() and koutecky_levich() separates mass-transport and kinetic limitations across rotation rates.
  • microdisc_limiting_current() and butler_volmer() provide fast analytical baselines for steady-state UMEs and interfacial kinetics.

# !pip install -q softpotato

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from softpotato import analytical as spa

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Shared parameters
n = 1
D_true = 8.5e-10
c_bulk = 1.0
area = 7.07e-6
nu = 1.0e-6
T = 298.15

# 1. Cottrell fit
t_ca = np.linspace(0.05, 4.0, 60)
i_ca = spa.cottrell(t_ca, n=n, D=D_true, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area) + rng.normal(
    0.0, 2.0e-7, size=t_ca.size
)
ca_fit = spa.fit_cottrell(t_ca, i_ca, n=n, area=area, c_bulk=c_bulk)
print(f"Cottrell fit: D = {ca_fit.d:.3e} +/- {ca_fit.d_stderr:.2e} m^2/s (true {D_true:.2e}), R^2 = {ca_fit.r_squared:.5f}")

# 2. Koutecky-Levich fit
rpm = np.array([400, 625, 900, 1225, 1600, 2025, 2500], dtype=float)
i_k_true = 1.0e-4  # 100 uA (mixed kinetic-diffusion regime)
i_kl = spa.koutecky_levich(
    rpm=rpm, i_k=i_k_true, n=n, D=D_true, c_bulk=c_bulk, area=area, nu=nu
) + rng.normal(0.0, 3.0e-7, size=rpm.size)
kl_fit = spa.fit_koutecky_levich(
    i_kl, rpm=rpm, method="nonlinear", n=n, area=area, c_bulk=c_bulk, nu=nu
)
print(f"K-L fit:      D = {kl_fit.d:.3e} m^2/s, I_k = {kl_fit.i_k*1e6:.2f} uA (true {i_k_true*1e6:.1f} uA), R^2 = {kl_fit.r_squared:.5f}")

# 3. Butler-Volmer fit
eta = np.linspace(-0.18, 0.18, 75)
i_bv = spa.butler_volmer(eta, i0=1.2e-5, alpha=0.42, n=n, T=T) + rng.normal(
    0.0, 8.0e-7, size=eta.size
)

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Use softpotato.analytical.fitting to extract physical parameters and 95% confidence intervals from noisy electrochemical datasets—both with specialized domain fitters (fit_cottrell, fit_koutecky_levich, fit_butler_volmer) and with the general-purpose fit_curve() API for custom nonlinear models.

docs.title: 2. Specialized Domain Fitters¶
docs.text: We generate synthetic noisy data for three canonical experiments and recover the underlying physical parameters with stderr and $R^2$ goodness-of-fit metrics.

docs.title: 3. Custom Nonlinear Model Fitting with fit_curve()¶
docs.text:
In real potential-step experiments, the measured current at short times is a superposition of Faradaic Cottrell diffusion and non-Faradaic double-layer charging:

$$ I(t) = \frac{k_{\text{Cot}}}{\sqrt{t}} + I_{\text{dl}} \exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau_{\text{RC}}}\right) $$

We use spa.fit_curve() with parameter bounds and param_names to deconvolve both contributions and inspect the residuals.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Specialized fitters (fit_cottrell, fit_koutecky_levich, fit_butler_volmer) return structured dataclasses with stderr, ci95, and r_squared.
  • fit_curve() wraps scipy.optimize.curve_fit with named parameters (param_names), bounds, and a unified FitResult container for arbitrary electrochemical models.

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Use PlanarGeometry, CylindricalGeometry, and SphericalGeometry directly inside DiffusionProblem to solve radial/linear diffusion, visualize 2D concentration profiles $c(r, t)$, and benchmark transient currents against analytical Cottrell equations.

docs.title: 2. Geometry Operators & Surface Areas¶
docs.text:
Each Geometry subclass encapsulates the coordinate metric $p \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ in the Laplacian:

$$ \nabla^2 c = \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial r^2} + \frac{p}{r}\frac{\partial c}{\partial r} $$

as well as area and surface_flux().

docs.title: 3. Solving Potential-Step Diffusion Across Geometries¶
docs.text: We apply a diffusion-limited Dirichlet boundary condition $c(r_0, t) = 0$ at the electrode surface and $c(r_{\max}, t) = c_{\text{bulk}}$ in the bulk, using a GeometricExpandingMesh that starts at $r_0$ (or $0$ for planar).

docs.title: 4. Concentration Profiles & Analytical Current Comparison¶
docs.text: We visualize $c_{\text{Ox}}(r, t)$ snapshots and heatmaps, and compare the simulated current densities against spa.cottrell(), spa.cottrell_cylinder(), and spa.cottrell_spherical().

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• PlanarGeometry, CylindricalGeometry, and SphericalGeometry plug directly into DiffusionProblem(..., geometry=...).
  • Radial convergence in cylindrical and spherical coordinates enhances mass transport at long times, matching cottrell_cylinder() and cottrell_spherical().

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Compare Uniform1DMesh, ExponentialMesh ("exponential", "tanh", "sinh"), and GeometricExpandingMesh, inspect their near-electrode resolution $\Delta x_0$, and run a quantitative grid-convergence study on the Cottrell potential-step problem.

docs.title: 2. Comparing Mesh Families¶
docs.text: In electrochemical simulations, concentration gradients are steepest right at the electrode surface ($x = 0$). Stretched meshes concentrate nodes near $x = 0$ while expanding smoothly into the bulk ($\delta = 6\sqrt{D t_{\max}}$).

docs.title: 3. Grid-Convergence Study: Uniform vs. Expanding Meshes¶
docs.text: Using softpotato.analytical.benchmark.run_cottrell_benchmark() and run_grid_efficiency_benchmark(), we measure how the relative $L_2$ current error scales with node count $N$ for uniform versus stretched meshes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• GeometricExpandingMesh and ExponentialMesh achieve orders-of-magnitude smaller boundary $\Delta x_0$ than Uniform1DMesh for the same node count $N$.
  • A 60-node stretched mesh routinely matches or beats a 400-node uniform mesh in Cottrell flux accuracy, yielding >5x speedups.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from softpotato.geometry import PlanarGeometry
from softpotato.grid import GeometricExpandingMesh

    ButlerVolmer,
    CustomMechanism,
    ElectrochemicalStep,
    FirstOrderReaction,
    SecondOrderReaction,
    Species,
)
from softpotato.solver import get_solver

D = 1.0e-9
c_bulk = 1.0
area = 7.07e-6
E_start, E_vertex, scan_rate = 0.4, -0.4, 0.2
t_total = 2.0 * abs(E_vertex - E_start) / scan_rate
t_half = abs(E_vertex - E_start) / scan_rate
def potential_fn(t: float) -> float:
    return E_start - scan_rate * t if t <= t_half else E_vertex + scan_rate * (t - t_half)
t_eval = np.linspace(0.0, t_total, 200)

ox = Species("Ox", diffusivity=D, bulk_concentration=c_bulk, standard_potential=0.0, n_electrons=1)
red = Species("Red", diffusivity=D, bulk_concentration=0.0)
prod = Species("P", diffusivity=D, bulk_concentration=0.0)

mesh = GeometricExpandingMesh.from_diffusion_layer(D=D, t_max=t_total, n_points=70, gamma=1.08)
geom = PlanarGeometry(area=area)
solver = get_solver("scipy_ivp", method="BDF", rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.5))
for k1 in [0.0, 0.5, 5.0]:
    reactions = [FirstOrderReaction(red, prod, k=k1)] if k1 > 0 else []
    mech = CustomMechanism(
        species=[ox, red, prod],
        reactions=reactions,
        electrochemical_steps=[
            ElectrochemicalStep(ox, red, ButlerVolmer(k0=1e-2, alpha=0.5, E0=0.0, n=1))
        ],
        name=f"EC (k1={k1})",
    )
    prob = mech.create_problem(mesh, potential=potential_fn, geometry=geom)
    res = solver.solve(prob, t_span=(0.0, t_total), t_eval=t_eval)
    E_arr = np.array([potential_fn(ti) for ti in t_eval])
    ax.plot(E_arr, res.currents["Ox"] * 1e6, label=rf"$k_1 = {k1}\ \mathrm{{s}}^{{-1}}$")

ax.set_xlabel("Potential $E$ [V]")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Current $I$ [$\mu$A]")
ax.set_title("Custom EC Mechanism via CustomMechanism + FirstOrderReaction")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: 1. Goal¶
docs.text: Construct custom chemical Species, interfacial ElectrochemicalSteps, and homogeneous FirstOrderReaction / SecondOrderReaction networks inside CustomMechanism, then solve the coupled reaction–diffusion PDE using Mechanism.create_problem() and get_solver("scipy_ivp").

docs.title: 2. Example A: First-Order EC Mechanism ($\text{Ox} + e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Red}$, $\text{Red} \xrightarrow{k_1} \text{P}$)¶
docs.text: We define three Species, a ButlerVolmer ElectrochemicalStep, and a FirstOrderReaction in CustomMechanism, and inspect how the homogeneous rate constant $k_1$ shifts the cyclic voltammogram.

docs.title: 3. Example B: Second-Order Homogeneous Reaction ($\text{Red} + \text{Z} \xrightarrow{k_2} \text{P}$)¶
docs.text: SecondOrderReaction(reactant_1, reactant_2, product, k) automatically provides both the nonlinear rate law $r = k_2 c_{\text{Red}} c_{\text{Z}}$ and its exact analytical local Jacobian to scipy_ivp (BDF/Radau). Here we simulate a potential step generating $\text{Red}$ that scavenges bulk species $\text{Z}$ in solution.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Species, ElectrochemicalStep, FirstOrderReaction, and SecondOrderReaction compose cleanly inside CustomMechanism.
  • mech.create_problem(...) builds a complete multi-species DiffusionProblem with automated boundary conditions and analytical reaction Jacobians for stiff ODE/DAE solvers (BDF / Radau).

docs.title: Low-Level PDE Solvers & Custom Boundary Conditions (softpotato.solver)¶
1. Goal¶
docs.text: Formulate DiffusionProblem directly with custom DirichletBC and NeumannBC conditions (including time-dependent BCs) and benchmark all four built-in PDE solvers: "explicit" (FTCS), "implicit" (BTCS), "crank_nicolson", and "scipy_ivp".

docs.title: 2. Canonical Fourier Decay: Comparing All Four Solvers¶
docs.text:
We solve the 1D diffusion equation on $x \in [0, 1]$ with $D = 0.05$:

$$ \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}, \quad c(0, t) = c(1, t) = 0, \quad c(x, 0) = \sin(\pi x) $$

whose exact analytical solution is $c_{\text{exact}}(x, t) = \sin(\pi x)\exp(-\pi^2 D t)$. Note that "explicit" (FTCS) enforces the CFL stability condition $r = D\,\Delta t / \Delta x^2 \le 0.5$.

docs.title: 4. Custom Time-Dependent Dirichlet & Neumann Boundary Conditions¶
docs.text: DirichletBC(callable) and NeumannBC(callable) accept any function f(t) of time. Here we impose a sinusoidal surface concentration at $x = 0$ and a zero-flux insulating wall (NeumannBC(0.0)) at $x = L$.

docs.title: Key Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• DiffusionProblem decouples the physical PDE (grid, diffusivity, BCs, ICs) from the numerical integrator (get_solver()).
  • "crank_nicolson" and "scipy_ivp" achieve 2nd-order or adaptive high accuracy without the restrictive CFL time-step limit of "explicit".
  • DirichletBC(fn) and NeumannBC(fn) support arbitrary time-dependent boundary forcing.
